In the South, rice and dal stick together even in conversations: arisi-paruppu in Tamil, akki-bele in Kannada, chorum-parippum in Malayalam, and pappu-annam in Telugu. I grew up loving paruppu. For as long as I can remember, breakfast was hot rice with a dollop of ghee and a ladle of creamy tovve ( toor ) dal. I’d mix it thoroughly and make a well in the centre, into which my grandmother would spoon some fresh cream-laced curd.
From breakfast to dinner, and dessert to round it off, dals hold an important position. Cutting across economic and social divides, it unites, acting as a thickener when meat is too expensive, and blending beautifully with vegetables and greens. “ Dals have always been one of the building blocks of South Indian cuisine. They not only lent protein, but also provided flavour,” says food historian Rakesh Raghunathan. “Each one has a certain texture and body, and a different use. Boiled toor and moong go into sambar , ground urad in idli , dosa and vadai , channa dal can be boiled, ground, roasted or fried for use in kootu, payasam , or podis . Each dal is versatile.” And becoming an adult and moving away from home usually coincides with a renewed love for this staple.
The five southern States grow and consume dal very differently. But the unifier is that it is a part of every meal. Intercropping with rice has meant there’s a predominance of pourable, scoopable preparations, while the varied regions and climates have dictated flavours. (The five States produce nearly 4 million tonnes of pulses annually, contributing to around 12% to 15% of India’s total pulse production.) For instance, Kerala and Karnataka often soften their dals with freshly grated coconut or coconut milk, but the other three turn to tamarind pulp, chillies and asafoetida for tangy heat.
“Food was never about human sustenance alone,” says cookbook author and food writer Mallika Badrinath; it was more ‘circular’. Earlier, urad dal , for instance, was soaked whole for idli and dosa , because “the green-black skin would be set aside for the cattle”. Native wisdom also dictated dishes. In Tamil cooking, different dals were cooked in specific combinations to ensure gut health — when it was not a fad, adds Badrinath.
In Karnataka, many of the indigenous communities have their own ways of cooking pulses. “This area is full of rain-fed lands, and dals and ragi are an integral part of the cultivation cycle and meal design,” says Vishalakshi Padmanabhan of Bengaluru-based Buffalo Back Collective, which works extensively with rural communities. “The Iruliga tribes routinely forage greens and tubers, and eat them with very specific combinations of dal . A certain bassaru [gravy] will only use avare bele [broad beans], another will only work with hurulikaalu [horse gram]. We are now trying to establish the bio-availability of these combinations using science.” This is similar to how the Mullu Kuruma and Kurichiya communities of Wayanad in Kerala combine green gram with tender colocasia leaves or wild amaranth.
